source.title: Advancing Neural Network Performance through Emergence-Promoting Initialization Scheme
source.authors: Johnny Jingze Li; V. George; Gabriel A. Silva

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is supplied.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether an initialization scheme changes early training performance, using first-epoch accuracy rather than training error or convergence time.
record.gate_note: The paper reports first-epoch accuracy comparisons in Table 1. It does not report training classification error, so those results do not test V1 or V3. ImageNet values are identified as results from Zhu et al. (2021), so they are not extracted as this study's results. The Transformer BLEU results do not measure the behaviors named in the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses established initialization and normalization findings to develop an emergence-promoting initialization scheme and reports its performance. It does not test whether activation-matched preservation of signals and gradients enables faster or deeper plain-network training (V4). Its BN comparisons change initialization scaling, and the conventional-initialization baselines are attributed to GradInit, so they do not establish this study's own controlled test of V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors claim improved accuracy and convergence speed from emergence-promoting initialization and recommend combining it with stability-promoting techniques, noting possible local-minimum trapping otherwise. These are the authors' claims; the comparisons do not isolate initialization from learning-rate choices, and Table 2 explicitly attributes its ImageNet results to Zhu et al. (2021).
record.recipe_differences: Changes layer-wise weight scaling after Kaiming or Xavier initialization to promote emergence; evaluates first-epoch accuracy and task performance, not training classification error.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that the scaling factor α depends on depth and learning rate, and that batch normalization stabilizes VGG-19 and permits larger α. Table 1 also separates BN and non-BN conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: The proposed emergence-promoting initialization reports higher first-epoch CIFAR-10 accuracy than the listed Kaiming baselines, using different learning-rate recipes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer-wise emergence-promoting weight scaling can improve early accuracy under the evaluated training recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report that BN stabilizes their scheme and permits larger α; the VGG comparison changes α from 2 without BN to 5 with BN.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch normalization can permit stronger emergence-promoting initialization scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: Transformer experiments report early BLEU improvements and best BLEU of 35.13 versus 34.78 for T-Fixup and 34.85 for Xavier.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emergence-promoting initialization can improve translation performance in the evaluated Post-LN Transformer recipes.

record.problems: The extracted CIFAR-10 table reports first-epoch accuracy rather than training error. The paper does not give α for the ResNet conditions in Table 1. ImageNet results are attributed to Zhu et al. (2021), rather than reported as this study's own results.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1's +1 epoch (Const. LR), +1 epoch (Warmup), and MetaInit cells are not extracted: they compare other initialization/training methods and are not needed for the tested version results retained here. Figure 3 and Table 2 are not extracted; Figure 3 reports plotted training loss/test accuracy without textual numeric results, and Table 2 is explicitly attributed to Zhu et al. (2021).

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error, corrupted or random labels, and dependence on size, stopping or regularization.
Teacher-student ReLU optimization, spurious minima frequency and student overparameterization.
Depth-dependent training degradation and matched identity-shortcut, tanh-initialization or Fixup comparisons.
Whether activation-matched preservation of signals and gradients speeds plain-network learning or increases trainable depth; orthogonal versus Gaussian weights and very deep convolutional networks.
Initial stability thresholds, transient loss increases, curvature evolution, recovery and divergence.
Controlled BN effects on accuracy acquisition and learning-rate tolerance, and the Fixup comparison. The qualitative stability observation and comparisons with changed α do not isolate these effects.

record.verdict_notes: First-epoch accuracy can inform early learning performance, but these method comparisons do not directly test the specific mechanisms and conditions in V4 or V6. The first-epoch T-Fixup BLEU values also differ between the prose and Table 3, so they should not be combined without clarification.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, random or corrupted labels, and the effects of model size, stopping, and regularization.
Teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Training error across depth with and without identity shortcuts, and the stated plain-network and normalization comparisons.
Activation-matched initialization, signal or gradient propagation, plain tanh depth, orthogonal weights, and 10,000-layer convolutional networks.
Learning rates above the stability threshold, curvature, and edge-of-stability behavior.
Tolerance of higher learning rates and the Fixup comparison without normalization.

relation.reason: Established initialization and BN findings motivate and support the method. Reported comparisons change initialization and learning-rate recipes; BN comparisons also change scaling, so they do not isolate the versions' effects.

tranche.reason: The study builds on stability-preserving initialization and normalization to develop its emergence-promoting method, reporting its own performance. It does not directly test the specified claim versions.

source_check.notes: All ten rows faithfully reproduce Table 1, but row eligibility remains a problem under the verdict rules. The supplied text is arXiv v3 dated January 2025; CIFAR-10 comparisons use different learning-rate recipes.
